title: Debt, taxes & firm value
description: Interest tax shields, WACC, and debt-funded buybacks.

questions.prompt: How much does interest reduce annual corporate taxes, in millions of dollars?
questions.context: A firm has $100 million of debt at 8% annual interest and a 25% corporate tax rate. Interest is fully deductible, and the firm has enough taxable income to use the deduction. Enter the number of millions.
questions.explanation: $2 million: annual interest is $8 million, and 25% of that is saved in taxes.
questions.detail: The annual interest tax shield is \(T_C r_D D\). Interest is \(0.08(100)=8\) million dollars, so the annual tax saving is \(0.25(8)=2\) million. Operating income is unchanged; total cash available to debt and equity rises because less goes to taxes.
questions.misconception: The deduction does not reimburse the full interest bill. The annual tax saving is also different from the present value of all future tax savings.

source.section: The Income Statement Secret: Where Does the Cash Go?; The Value of the Interest Tax Shield
source.textbook: Ross, Westerfield & Jordan, Fundamentals of Corporate Finance, 13th ed. — Chapter 16

questions.prompt: What is the levered firm value, in millions of dollars?
questions.context: An unlevered firm is worth $360 million. It issues $160 million of permanent debt and pays all proceeds to shareholders. The corporate tax rate is 25%. Operations stay unchanged; deductions are fully usable, tax-shield risk equals debt risk, and there are no other financing costs. Enter the number of millions.
questions.explanation: $400 million: the $360 million operating value plus a $40 million tax shield.
questions.detail: Under these permanent-debt assumptions, \(PV(\text{tax shield})=T_C D=0.25(160)=40\) million dollars. Thus \(V_L=V_U+T_C D=360+40=400\) million. After the payout, equity is worth \(E=400-160=240\) million; debt and equity together are worth 400 million.
questions.misconception: The $160 million borrowed is not free wealth. It creates a debt claim and is paid out; the value gain here is the $40 million tax shield.

questions.prompt: What is the firm’s after-tax WACC?
questions.context: Market values are $200 million of equity and $200 million of debt. Equity requires 18%, debt requires 8%, and the corporate tax rate is 25%. Assume the interest deduction is fully usable. Enter a percentage.
questions.explanation: 12%: the weighted equity cost is 9%, and the weighted after-tax debt cost is 3%.
questions.detail: Both market-value weights are one-half. The after-tax debt cost is \(8\%(1-0.25)=6\%\). Therefore \(\mathrm{WACC}=0.5(18\%)+0.5(6\%)=12\%\). Apply this rate to unlevered free cash flow; adding the tax shield to that cash flow again would double-count the tax benefit.
questions.misconception: Apply the tax adjustment to debt, not equity. Use D/(D+E) for the debt weight, not D/E.

questions.prompt: What is the share price immediately after the announcement, in dollars?
questions.context: An all-equity firm worth $480 million has 12 million shares. It unexpectedly announces a credible $120 million permanent-debt buyback. The tax rate is 20%; operations are unchanged, deductions are fully usable, tax-shield risk equals debt risk, and there are no other financing costs. Prices immediately reflect the plan, before any debt is issued or shares repurchased.
questions.explanation: $42: the original $40 price rises by $2 per share as the $24 million tax shield is priced in.
questions.detail: The tax shield is \(0.20(120)=24\) million dollars. Before debt issuance or repurchase, all 12 million original shares share the gain: \(P=(480+24)/12=42\) dollars. Sellers and continuing shareholders both benefit when the later repurchase takes place at the fair post-announcement price.
questions.misconception: Use the original share count for the announcement gain. The debt proceeds themselves are not an additional $120 million of shareholder wealth.

questions.prompt: Why does the tax benefit not justify unlimited real-world borrowing?
questions.context: The tax-only MM model gives permanent debt a value benefit when interest deductions are fully usable.

options.text: Expected distress costs and unusable tax deductions can offset the benefit.
Debt eliminates the firm’s operating risk.
Each borrowed dollar is a free dollar of firm value.
Interest always reduces taxes dollar for dollar.

questions.explanation: Tax shields are only part of the decision. Distress costs and limited taxable income can reduce the net benefit.
questions.detail: The formula \(V_L=V_U+T_C D\) assumes usable interest deductions and no offsetting financing costs. More debt can make costly distress more likely, while a firm without enough taxable income may not use deductions when expected. These departures can make additional borrowing unattractive.
questions.misconception: A model’s prediction is conditional on its assumptions. The tax-only benchmark does not establish an unlimited borrowing policy for actual firms.
